news.title: Gold falls below $3,900 as December Fed hike bets build, Warsh in focus
Iran’s navy says three tankers on fire after hitting mines in Hormuz
Goldman sees Brent at $78 by end-2027 as oil surplus returns, flags near-term upside risk
body: Goldman’s path implies Brent averaging nearly $8 below current levels next year, and about $18 lower by end-2027. That gives oil bears a solid medium-term anchor. In the near term, though, the market is still driven by the war. Confirmation of the IRGC’s tanker-sinking claims could quickly rebuild the risk premium that Goldman expects to fade. Monday’s dip suggests traders are leaning toward the surplus story for now. The diesel forecast matters for inflation. At $150 a barrel, products stay costly even as crude eases, so energy keeps feeding into the inflation concerns Fed officials raised over the weekend.
Goldman’s message on oil is patience: a surplus is coming and prices should fall, but until the Gulf calms down, the risks over the next few weeks still point upward.

Goldman Sachs expects oil prices to drift lower over the next year as the market returns to surplus. It forecasts Brent crude to average $88 a barrel in 2027 and ease to $78 by December 2027, though it warned of upside risks in the near term from attacks on shipping in the Middle East, Reuters reported.

For US crude, the bank sees West Texas Intermediate averaging $78 a barrel next year and slipping to $70 by the end of 2027. Refined products should also ease but stay well above historical norms, with US wholesale diesel forecast to average $150 a barrel in 2027.

The core of the call is supply. In Goldman’s base case, oil production will exceed end-use demand by 2 million barrels per day in 2027. That surplus is large enough to pull prices down from current levels, even if some war-related risk premium lingers.

The bank was careful to present the risks as running in both directions. In the near term, it said prices could rise if attacks on shipping intensify, if oil infrastructure is damaged or if the risk premium rebuilds. Over the medium term, the risk is to the downside, through stronger supply, weaker demand or a smaller risk premium than it assumes.

That near-term risk is real. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed over the weekend that two tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz and that one of them, a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels, sank. There has been no independent confirmation.

Even so, prices fell on Monday on expectations of a supply surplus. Shipments through Hormuz were reported to be close to pre-war levels, and Washington eased domestic fuel movements by extending its Jones Act waiver. Brent was trading around $95.50 earlier in Asia, well above Goldman’s 2027 average, which implies significant downside if the bank’s surplus view plays out.
The gap between today’s prices and the forecast path leaves the oil market hinging on one question: whether supply disruption in the Gulf fades or flares up again.

news.title: Japan economy shrinks 0.1% in Q3, first fall in 4 quarters as inflation hits households
body: The pushback from economists matters more for markets than the headline miss. If weak consumption is read as a sign of inflation rather than a reason to pause, December hike pricing should hold. That limits any lasting yen weakness from the data, although USD/JPY near 160 remains in intervention territory. The risk lies in the board split some economists flagged. Further soft consumption data could give the doves more influence and push hike timing back, which would weigh on the yen and lift JGBs. Oil is the link in the middle. Energy-driven inflation is both hurting households and pushing the BOJ to tighten, so higher crude makes the policy dilemma worse.
Japan’s shoppers are buckling under inflation, but rather than giving the BOJ a reason to pause, the squeeze on households is being read as further proof that rates need to keep rising.

Japan’s economy unexpectedly contracted in the July to September quarter as rising living costs forced households to cut back on spending. Economists say the weakness is unlikely to knock the Bank of Japan off its tightening path, Reuters reported.

Gross domestic product fell an annualised 0.1%, against a median forecast of 0.3% growth, following an upwardly revised 1.7% expansion in the previous quarter. It was the first contraction in four quarters. On a quarterly basis, output slipped 0.02%, versus expectations of a 0.1% rise.

Households did most of the damage. Private consumption, which makes up more than half of economic output, fell 0.3%, slightly worse than the expected 0.2% drop. Persistent inflation, heavy rain and typhoons weighed on spending. Purchases of cars and air conditioners also fell back after a temporary boost from tax and regulatory changes in the prior quarter. Economists warned that higher prices linked to Middle East tensions will keep squeezing households’ purchasing power, even as wages rise.

Trade also took away from growth. Net external demand cut 0.6 percentage point, more than the expected 0.4 point drag. Imports jumped as oil and other energy purchases recovered after Japan diversified its supply following disruption from the war in the Middle East.
Business investment was the bright spot. It rose 1.6% against a 1.5% forecast, supported by spending on labour-saving technology and AI-related projects.

Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi said better employment and income conditions, along with policy measures, should support a gradual recovery, but stressed the need to monitor the Middle East situation closely.

For the BOJ, which raised rates in June and September, economists say the miss changes little. Several argued that weak consumption is itself a symptom of high prices, which strengthens the case for further hikes, and many expect the next move as soon as December. One note cautioned, however, that if consumer weakness persists, it could widen divisions on the board and give more dovish members grounds to argue for caution.
That debate gets an early test later on Monday, when hawkish board member Hajime Takata speaks at 04:00 GMT (11:00 pm ET Sunday).

news.title: Gold slips toward $3,876 ahead of Warsh as Fed speakers line up behind tighter policy
body: How the market reacts to Warsh will depend on tone more than detail. If he gives weight to AI as a future disinflationary force, traders could read it as a reason the Fed can stop after a few more hikes. That would offer relief to front-end Treasury yields and to gold. If he echoes Schmid’s view that AI demand responds to rates, it backs a longer tightening cycle and supports the US dollar. Gold remains the most exposed asset. With ETF selling risk now flagged and $4,000 broken, a hawkish lean could extend losses quickly. For equities, his comments on AI land the day before Nvidia’s results and will feed straight into how investors value the AI trade.

-- Warsh has staked part of his Fed leadership on the idea that AI can ease inflation, and on Monday he makes that case to a room of colleagues who have spent the past few days warning it is doing the opposite.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh gives opening remarks at the Fed’s Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference on Monday at 17:00 GMT (12:00 pm ET), hosted by the San Francisco Fed. The appearance follows a run of hawkish commentary from his colleagues over the past few days, and a December rate increase is widely expected.

The forum will bring together technology executives, economists and employers to examine whether artificial intelligence will lower inflation, push prices higher or displace workers. It is the first major public event for one of five task forces Warsh set up after taking office in May. He flagged it in October, when he described the surge in AI investment as one of the factors behind higher inflation. Warsh has argued that AI could eventually help firms produce more at lower cost and ease price pressure. Some colleagues see the AI boom adding to inflation today, with the productivity gains still unproven.

That debate has been front and centre in recent days. Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid said inflation is uncomfortably above target and heading the wrong way, and rejected the idea that AI-driven demand is beyond the reach of higher rates. Boston Fed President Susan Collins backed a steady, gradual pace of hikes, but said the eventual rate path may end up higher than she had expected. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said the trajectory of inflation is the most important signal for policy, and warned that higher energy prices risk a broader rise, with PCE inflation at 3.6% in September.
The Fed raised rates to a 3.75% to 4.00% range in September and held in October. Markets are fully priced for a quarter-point increase on December 8-9, with a small chance of a larger move.

Gold has taken the brunt of that hawkish shift. The metal slipped in Asian trade to around $3,876 an ounce, extending a slide of almost 7% since last Tuesday, after Goldman Sachs cut its end-2027 forecast to $4,650 from $4,800 on expectations of a further hike in March 2027.

Opening remarks at a themed conference may carry little direct policy guidance, and Warsh said in October that he does not prejudge meetings. Any comment on AI’s effect on inflation, however, will be read for clues about December. Fed minutes follow on Wednesday at 19:00 GMT.

news.title: Goldman’s second gold forecast downgrade in a month turns its bear case into the base case
body: For gold, the near-term risk is a self-reinforcing slide. If ETF holders start to sell, losses could build regardless of the macro backdrop, and $4,000, the support that has now broken, becomes resistance on any bounce. The main swing factor is Fed pricing. Any sign that December could bring a half-point hike, or that March 2027 is firmly on the table, would add pressure. A softer US data run could ease it. Oil remains an indirect headwind. Higher crude tied to the Iran war lifts inflation and rate expectations, so escalation in the Gulf has been negative for gold rather than supportive. Longer-term buyers may see Goldman’s 16% upside call as a reason to accumulate gradually on weakness.
Goldman’s second downgrade and warnings of ETF selling point to the same problem for gold: a Fed that keeps hiking leaves little room for a quick recovery, even with central banks still buying.

Goldman Sachs has lowered its end-2027 gold price forecast to $4,650 an ounce from $4,800, its second downgrade in a month, as expectations of a longer run of Federal Reserve rate hikes cloud the outlook for investor demand, Investing.com reported.

The bank’s economists now expect the Fed to deliver a third quarter-point increase in March 2027, on top of the December hike that was already in Goldman’s base case. A rising policy rate is likely to weigh on private-sector investment in gold through early next year, even as central banks keep buying. In practice, the new target lines up with the bear-case scenario Goldman flagged in its previous note, which effectively moves that outcome into the main forecast.

Goldman’s first cut, earlier this month, lowered its end-2026 target to $4,150 from $4,650 and its end-2027 target to $4,800 from $5,400. The bank remains constructive over the longer run. It expects central banks to buy around 60 tonnes a month through 2026 and 2027. It still sees roughly 16% upside from current prices by December 2027, once the Fed starts cutting rates late next year and private demand returns.

The near-term picture is more fragile. Gold has fallen almost 7%, or about $290, since last Tuesday and is trading around $3,890. Analysts at a major European bank noted that rate expectations and bond yields have not risen enough over that time to fully explain the slide. They warned that exchange-traded fund investors could start selling into the weakness, which would push prices lower still. That is a risk rather than a confirmed wave of outflows, but it marks a shift from late October, when the same analysts described gold’s drop as excessive.

The common thread is the Fed. Hot inflation, and talk from some officials of a larger hike next month, have hardened the market’s hawkish bias. Higher oil prices tied to the Middle East conflict have fed that view rather than supporting gold as a haven.
Near-term tests include US retail sales and industrial production on Tuesday, and the minutes of the Fed’s latest meeting on November 18.

news.title: ICYMI: Fed’s Jefferson says inflation is the key signal for rates, with PCE still at 3.6%
body: Jefferson’s comments support pricing for a December hike without adding to the half-point tail, which suits the steady, gradual camp. By naming energy as the main channel for broader inflation, he makes Fed expectations sensitive to oil. Any renewed jump in crude tied to the Iran war and Hormuz shipping risk would feed quickly into rate pricing and the US dollar. His upbeat view on growth and jobs also removes an easy reason to pause. That keeps front-end Treasury yields supported, and continues to put gold under pressure from the Fed’s tightening path.
With unemployment steady and growth near potential, Jefferson has made it plain that inflation, and energy-driven inflation in particular, now sets the Fed’s course.

Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said the path of inflation, rather than growth or jobs, will be the main guide for future interest rate decisions, as price pressures remain well above the central bank’s 2% target.

Speaking at the University of California, San Diego Economic Roundtable on Friday, Jefferson said further policy moves should be decided by carefully weighing trends in the data, the changing outlook and the balance of risks, ANI reported. He described inflation’s trajectory as the more important signal for setting the stance of policy.

Figures cited in his speech showed headline personal consumption expenditures inflation at 3.6% in September, with core PCE, which strips out food and energy, at 3.1%. Jefferson said the October inflation data received so far point to price pressures staying well above target.

He flagged energy as the main risk. Jefferson said he remains concerned that higher energy prices could lead to a broader and more persistent rise in inflation, noting that the effect is already visible in airfares and transport costs. Strong demand for new technologies is also lifting prices of some goods, including memory chips.

By contrast, his assessment of the real economy was steady. Jefferson said labour market conditions have stabilised, with unemployment at 4.1% in October, a level he regards as consistent with maximum employment and expects to hold in the near term. The economy has gained momentum this year, he said, with third-quarter GDP growing at an annualised 3.4%, roughly in line with its potential.

Jefferson said he voted with the majority to hold rates at the Federal Open Market Committee’s October meeting. Since then, he said, activity and the labour market have remained broadly solid, while inflation readings have continued to show persistent pressure.

As vice chair, Jefferson’s views carry weight with the committee’s centre. By putting inflation ahead of a stable labour market, his remarks fit the Fed’s tightening bias, with markets widely expecting a quarter-point rate increase at the December meeting. Upcoming core PCE data will be a key test of that view.

news.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6771 – Reuters estimate
body: The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets.

China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours.

Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations.

Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.

In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

news.title: US futures open firmer as Nasdaq leads, oil slips despite Iran tanker claims: 5 things
body: The opening tone is cautiously risk-on, but thin early liquidity means these moves are a tentative read rather than a settled direction. Oil’s restraint is the notable signal. With three US carrier groups now in the region and Iran claiming more mine strikes, the risk premium is skewed upward if any tanker sinking is independently confirmed, so dips in crude look vulnerable to headline risk. In FX, USD/JPY is pressing toward 160, which keeps yen intervention risk alive just as Japanese GDP lands and BoJ hawk Takata speaks later in the session. Gold remains caught between geopolitical tension and a Fed on a hiking path, and the hiking path is winning for now.
Futures have shrugged off a weekend of Iranian tanker claims, Nvidia leadership drama and hawkish Fed talk, with tech leading the early bid and oil waiting for proof before it reacts.

US stock index futures opened the new week on the front foot in early Asia-Pacific trade on Monday, led by technology. Oil prices edged lower even after Iran claimed fresh mine strikes on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend. Prices below are as of around 23:40 GMT (6:40 pm ET on Sunday).

Equities S&P 500 futures were up about 0.3% near 7,603, and Nasdaq 100 futures gained around 0.6% to roughly 28,200. The tech bid comes despite a turbulent weekend for Nvidia, after a Financial Times report that former chief executive Jensen Huang is weighing a return to the company days after resigning. Nvidia reports results on Tuesday under an interim chief, which makes it the week’s key event for the AI trade. Signs of strain in AI financing are also worth watching, after Blackstone-backed data center operator QTS cut a planned debt sale by about 60%.

Oil Brent slipped around 0.7% to near $95.50, and WTI was little changed near $87. Iran has claimed that a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels sank after hitting a mine. The muted reaction suggests traders are waiting for independent confirmation, after a series of similar announcements from Tehran in recent weeks. Separately, the USS Theodore Roosevelt has reportedly arrived in the Middle East. It joins the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington, giving the US three carrier strike groups in the region.
Gold Gold was little changed around $3,890 an ounce, with hawkish Fed commentary over the weekend keeping a lid on gains.
Bitcoin Bitcoin rose nearly 2% to around $65,300, outperforming other risk assets in early trade.

What’s ahead The Fed is widely expected to raise rates by a quarter point at its December 8-9 meeting. Over the weekend, Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid said the Fed has work to do on inflation, while Boston Fed President Susan Collins backed a steady, gradual pace of hikes. Upcoming US core PCE price data will be watched closely for confirmation. In Asia, Japan’s preliminary third-quarter GDP is due shortly, followed by China’s October activity data.
